content: Is it going to compete with Lean Pool in terms of attention and token consumption?

Sorry, I should write separately something about the distinction between Lean Pool and Tau Ceti.

The basic difference is that Tau Ceti is library, and is explicitly intended to produce its content via AI, while Lean Pool is an archive of independent projects (and, as far as I'm aware, is in principle AI agnostic).

I see Lean Pool as aiming at an "AfP for Lean".

I think both projects can coexist and supplement each other! Lean Pool can catch many useful things where the authors don't have the time/skill/inclination to preprare Tau Ceti suitable roadmaps and then get their work through the Tau Ceti review process. Tau Ceti can add additional value to projects that already exist separately (and are possibly included in Lean Pool), by integrating them into a more coherent library (and in particular, making sure there is no duplication with Tau Ceti and Mathlib), and bringing them up to the "survives Tau Ceti's adversarial review process" standard.

My understanding is that TauCeti is a bit more controlled/curated than LeanPool (which closer to the merely-true end of the spectrum).

Vasily seems to be by accepting almost any project in #AI authored projects channel to LeanPool--focusing on quantity over quality. TauCeti requires all PRs to start from a human-audited roadmap, and uses very specific review prompts/harness for PRs.

@Jack McCarthy , If we had an objective measure of quality, I would not be surprised if Lean Pool was higher than TauCeti. Not because my AI review is better than Kim's AI review, but because half of Lean Pool consists of human-written projects. Lean Pool is easy to audit, because each project has a specific named theorem or paper it formalizes. I've rejected several PRs that did not have such a named result. If a lemma is used in a proof of a significant result, it's not a completely useless lemma. Lean Pool is very far from merely-true.

TauCeti is harder to audit, it requires creating a roadmap, and even then it's hard to tell whether the resulting code is good. I am attempting to do it with my statistical approach to code quality (#AI authored projects > Statistical approach to code quality) because otherwise we are supposed to just trust that the 100k lines of completely LLM-generated code makes a good library. I am an AI optimist but I don't have as much trust in today's LLMs' ability to design a good library as Kim does.

My mental model for Lean Pool is that it's like arXiv. There is a small amount of moderation that goes a long way, and each project is like a paper. I hope that in the near future each arXiv math paper comes with a formalization, and Lean Pool will be a natural place to put these formalizations. I guess TauCeti is what the formalization landscape would look like if AI became as good as it is today 10 years earlier, before mathlib existed.
See https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-pool#difference-from-similar-projects for a comparison of Lean Pool and TauCeti.

@Vasily Ilin Yeah, I was wrong to say quantity over quality. As of July 21st, we have no idea which approach will produce a highest quality library in the end (whatever that means).
I want to clarify also I'm not trying to critique Lean Pool at all-- I think Lean Pool and TauCeti are both important, parallel experiments for the community.

But maybe I still don't understand your distinction from merely-true. As far as I can tell, Lean Pool is willing to accept almost any project as long as it meets a basic threshold--i.e. a significant target theorem + pass CI. This is not drastically different from merely-true which asked for passing CI + a few other small quality checks. I agree Lean Pool can serve a similar service as arXiv, or Isabelle's Afp as Kim noted above.
I think it is best to move this convo to a new thread specifically for discussing the distinction between these two repos.

@Jack McCarthy , merely-true accepted things like https://github.com/merely-true/merely-true/pull/14/changes. It would have also accepted a PR that had max_heartbeats set to 10_000_000, and a hundred proofs of True. I want an arXiv-like model. Papers on arXiv are not as high quality as in Journals (although there is a good amount of overlap) but there are not many arXiv papers that are complete nonsense. Lean Pool does not aim to build a mathlib-like library (that's harder, TauCeti is doing it and I think it's going fantastic). Lean Pool aims to preserve one-off formalization projects that others might want to build on. If TauCeti is a densely connected graph, Lean Pool is more like a fractal: probably no project will depend on two projects, because they are likely incompatible due to the level of generality but it can depend on a single existing project (perhaps after a small refactor).

Example: as math paper 1 gets on arXiv, and its formalization F1 gets in Lean Pool, I hope that paper 2 that builds on paper 1's results will reuse parts of F1 in its formalization F2 and F2 will also get in Lean Pool. There might also be paper 3, which also depends on paper 1, and whose formalization F3 also depends on F1, so the project-level dep graph might look like
F2
/
F1
\
F3
